body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Structured video debriefing with a coach and laparoscopic skill scores in general surgery residents over one academic year","authors":"Ferrante-Osei L, Kowalczyk-Adams M, Nwachukwu-Berg T","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Operative Training","doi":"10.5555/jot.2022.0131","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 36 general surgery residents in two programmes through one academic year. Twenty residents chose to take part in monthly video debriefing of a filmed laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a trained consultant coach; 16 did not. Two blinded raters scored one video per resident at the start and end of the year with a five-domain global rating scale (score 5 to 25). Scores rose by a mean of 4.1 points in coached residents and 2.3 points in residents who were not coached, a difference of 1.8 points (95 percent CI 0.4 to 3.2) after adjustment for training year. Residents who chose coaching had higher baseline scores, and self-selection may explain part of the difference."},{"title":"Reliability of blinded video rating of laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a global rating scale","authors":"Lindgren-Achebe S, Moreau-Tan J","year":2019,"venue":"Surgical Education Methods","doi":"10.5555/sem.2019.0047","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Operative skill is often judged by the supervising surgeon, who knows the trainee. We asked three surgeons who did not know the trainees to rate 60 edited videos of laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a five-domain global rating scale. Inter-rater reliability was good (intraclass correlation 0.79 for the total score), and two raters were enough for decisions about change over time. Rating one video took about 12 minutes once the video had been edited to the critical steps. Reliability was lower for the domain on flow of the operation. Unedited full-length videos took three times as long to rate without improving agreement."},{"title":"Peer versus consultant video coaching for surgical trainees: a randomised comparison","authors":"Adeyemi-Sato K, Brennan-Iqbal R, Holm-Mensah D","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Operative Training","doi":"10.5555/jot.2024.0019","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Forty-eight residents were randomly allocated to video coaching by a senior peer or by a consultant for six months, with one coaching session a month. Both groups improved on blinded global rating scale scores, by 3.6 points with peer coaching and 3.9 points with consultant coaching, a difference within the pre-specified margin of 1.5 points. Consultant sessions lasted a mean of 45 minutes and peer sessions 35 minutes. There was no group without coaching, so the study cannot show whether coaching itself improves skill. Loss to follow-up was 10 percent, mostly residents who changed rotation."},{"title":"Residents' views on filming their operations for coaching and assessment in three training programmes","authors":"O'Rourke-Diallo P, Vasquez-Lund H","year":2018,"venue":"Surgical Education Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 112 surgical residents in three programmes about filming and reviewing their operations; 81 responded. Most (72 percent) were willing to have operations filmed for coaching, but only 38 percent were willing for the same videos to be used in formal assessment. Residents worried about who could see the videos and how long they were kept. Female residents and junior residents were more likely to worry that videos would be used against them. Willingness was higher when the resident could choose which cases to film and when videos were deleted after review."},{"title":"Video coaching and intraoperative autonomy ratings in junior surgical residents","authors":"Nakamura-Pryce E, Okafor-Stein B","year":null,"venue":"Proceedings of the Surgical Training Forum","providerType":"conference-abstract","abstract":"Junior residents who received three video coaching sessions were compared with junior residents in the same programme who did not. Attending surgeons rated intraoperative autonomy on a four-level scale after each operation. Coached residents reached the level of performing the operation with passive help earlier, after a median of 14 operations against 19 operations for residents who were not coached. Raters were not blinded to coaching, the number of residents is not reported in the abstract, and the conference listing gives no year of presentation."}]}
